/learn/system-design/advertising-platfor.text: Harness/System design/Advertising platforms In this guide 01Start with the user experience 02From setting up an ad to reading the report 03What to ask about each platform 04Connect your own software to a platform 05Start with ChatGPT Ads Back to the track System design · Platform overview How advertising platforms work 7 min readUpdated 7 November 2026 An advertising platform brings a campaign into something a person is already doing, such as searching, watching a video or asking for advice. How the platform picks and shows an ad affects what you can learn from the campaign report. On this page 01Start with the user experience 02From setting up an ad to reading the report 03What to ask about each platform 04Connect your own software to a platform 05Start with ChatGPT Ads Use this guide to Follow an ad from campaign setup to the performance report. See which actions show up in the data you can collect. Choose what to explore next, from collecting reports to testing campaign changes. Access No account or API key is needed for this guide. No installation is needed to read this guide. Start with the user experience Begin with what the person is doing: searching for an answer, watching a video, browsing a feed, comparing a product or asking for advice. An ad occupies a particular place in that experience. Where the ad appears shapes what it can look like, what people can do with it and what you can measure. Ask where an ad can appear, which ads qualify and which settings you can change. Then check what the platform counts. An impression records an ad being shown. A conversion is an action you measure, such as a purchase or signup. Each platform has its own rules for counting them. From setting up an ad to reading the report A simplified view of how advertising works 01Set up the campaign 02Choose and show ads 03Measure what people do 04Review results You set the campaign goal, choose the ad content (the creative), set limits on who can see it and decide how much to spend. The platform chooses which ad to show from the ones that qualify. It records actions and groups them into results you can use. Results feed back into later decisions about bids, budgets and ads. How useful they are depends on your goal, how well the numbers capture it, how quickly they arrive and which settings you can change. What to check before using a report When you pull reports into your own tools, check what each number means, whether you have every batch and whether recent figures might change. What to ask about each platform Scroll across to compare all columns → Platform Where people see ads Questions to ask Google Ads Search, YouTube and other places Google shows ads. How do campaign type and placement affect where ads show, how reports group results and which metrics you can compare? Meta Advertising within social experiences, including Facebook and Instagram. How do the ad, campaign goal and measured actions relate to the results in the report? Amazon Ads Advertising around shopping and media experiences. What can you learn from campaign reports, and when do you need to combine data or build audiences? TikTok Ads as people discover and watch videos. Which views, interactions and later actions can your software collect? ChatGPT Ads Advertising in the context of exploration and decisions in a conversation. How are ads chosen, what can advertisers change and what can they measure? Programmatic: DV360 & The Trade Desk Buying and measuring ads across many publishers’ sites and apps. Which tools let you set up campaigns, create reports and download every batch of results? Use these questions to compare platforms. Check each platform’s rules for choosing ads, organising campaigns and deciding which ads get credit for a conversion. Amazon Marketing Cloud helps advertisers analyse data and build audiences alongside their campaign reports. It’s a clean room, a controlled space for working with data under privacy rules. Amazon Marketing Cloud overview Connect your own software to a platform Setting up ads, sending records of actions and collecting performance results are separate jobs. They may use different APIs, which are the ways your software asks the platform for data or actions. For example, Google directs DV360 performance reporting to the Bid Manager API. Campaign management uses the Display & Video 360 API. DV360 reporting boundary Choose the account and dates. Decide how to group results, such as by campaign and day, and check each metric’s units and meaning. Keep track of which batches you’ve collected, which reports are still running and why any data is missing. Save the original results, avoid counting a record twice and make it possible to pick up after an interruption. Flag late or revised data. A successful request can return figures that will still change. When you use a report to make a decision, explain what it covers and what is still uncertain. Pagination fetches the next batch of the same report. Splitting a request asks for several smaller reports. Streaming lets you read a large file as it arrives. Whichever approach you use, check that you have every batch you asked for. Start with ChatGPT Ads The ChatGPT Ads guide follows an ad from the conversation where it might appear to the report an advertiser can read. The reporting example shows how your software can ask for daily campaign results and flag gaps. Start with the platform guide to see how the parts fit together. If you’re already working on a reporting tool, start with the API design principles. Where to go next Related guides Platform introduction How ChatGPT Ads works See how ChatGPT Ads chooses and shows ads, what advertisers can control and what reports can tell you. Reusable principles API design principles Define what someone can ask an API to do, who has permission, and how to tell whether the task is finished. Platform sources Official sources used in this guide. Check your own ad account for the features you can access. /learn/system-design/api-design.title: API design principles · Harness · AI Knowledge Hub
/learn/system-design/api-design.description: Define what someone can ask an API to do, who has permission, and how to tell whether the task is finished.
/learn/system-design/api-design.text: Harness/System design/API design In this guide 01Start with the task 02Define the contract 03Keep the meaning when data moves 04Make failures useful 05Apply the principles in a case Back to the track System design · Reusable principles API design principles 8 min readUpdated 8 November 2026 An API (application programming interface) gives software a way to ask another system for data or to take an action. A good API tells you what you can ask for, what will change and what the result actually shows. Read these guides in any order API principlesDesign a clear request How ads workSee how ads are chosen Advertiser APIsFind the tool you need Reporting exampleCollect campaign results On this page 01Start with the task 02Define the contract 03Keep the meaning when data moves 04Make failures useful 05Apply the principles in a case Use this guide to Describe the task before choosing how to run it. Explain what the task covers, what it changes and when it is done. Use the same rules when a person, an app or an AI agent runs the task. Before you start The examples use HTTP, the rules software follows to send a request over the web and receive a reply. No account or API key is needed for this guide. No installation is needed to read this guide. Start with the task Write down who is making the request, what it covers and what they should get back. “Get last week’s campaign results” and “change the campaign budget” can use the same API. One reads data and the other changes a setting. What happens when you ask an API to do something 01Define the task 02Check permissions and details 03Run the task within its limits 04Explain the result Put permission checks and limits in the code that runs the task. Those rules should apply whether someone uses a web request, a command-line interface (CLI) for typed commands, or an AI agent connected through the Model Context Protocol (MCP). Define the contract A contract is the set of rules a request and its result must follow. For a report, it covers details such as who can ask for it, which dates it includes and how to tell whether data is missing. Part of the contract What to decide Identity and permission Who can make the request, which accounts or records they can use, and where the system checks permission. Inputs What you must supply, what the system assumes if you leave something blank, and which units and dates it accepts. Effects Whether the task reads data or changes it, and how to check what happened. Results How to tell a finished task from an empty result, a partial result, a refused request or a service that could not respond. Limits How much work the system will do, how long it will wait and how to continue or stop. Source of the data Where the data came from, when it was recorded, what was changed and what is still uncertain. A server can successfully receive a request while the report is still being prepared. A valid account ID can belong to someone else. Make the result say whether the task is finished and whether the requester has permission. Keep the meaning when data moves If you reformat a report or calculate a new metric, keep the original IDs and units alongside the result. Mark an unavailable number as missing so readers can distinguish it from a measured zero. For a list or report, explain how results are ordered and how to tell when you have the last batch. For a change such as a budget update, explain how to recognise a repeat request. If the first attempt times out, check whether it took effect before trying again. Give your report format a version so readers and software know how to interpret it. If you change what a field means, use a new version and explain the change. For example, a report grouped by the date of an ad interaction answers a different question from one grouped by the date of a purchase. Make failures useful Condition What the result should tell you Empty The system checked the requested account, dates or records and found no matches. Partial Which results are available, which are missing and how to continue or why the task stopped. Rejected What was wrong with the request or which permission is needed. Keep passwords, keys and private data out of the message. Unavailable Whether you can safely try again, how many attempts to make and where to pick up. Unconfirmed change A request ID and a way to check whether the change happened before you repeat it. Give people a short explanation. Give apps and agents a consistent code for each reason and a clear next step. Apply the principles in a case The ChatGPT Ads reporting case shows how these rules work in practice. You choose the account and dates, collect every batch of results and make any gaps visible in the report. Find the API you need Use the advertiser API guide to find the right tool. Open the reporting example for a sample request. The platform guide explains how ads are chosen, shown and measured. Next · Worked example · Preview How to collect ChatGPT Ads reports Apply the contract to a daily campaign report and see how the response explains missing data. Read the reporting case Where to go next Related guides Advertiser API guide ChatGPT Ads APIs for advertisers See which ChatGPT Ads tools let you set up ads, send conversion data and read performance reports. /learn/system-design/chatgpt-ads-apis.description: See which ChatGPT Ads tools let you set up ads, send conversion data and read performance reports.
/learn/system-design/chatgpt-ads-apis.text: Harness/System design/Advertiser APIs In this guide 01What advertisers can do 02How to read the internal tools in our examples 03API documentation and downloads Back to the track System design · Advertiser API guide ChatGPT Ads APIs for advertisers 6 min readUpdated 8 November 2026 Use this map to find the tool for your task. An API is how your software asks a platform for data or sends it instructions. ChatGPT Ads has separate tools for changing ad settings, sending records of actions like purchases and reading campaign results. Read these guides in any order API principlesDesign a clear request How ads workSee how ads are chosen Advertiser APIsFind the tool you need Reporting exampleCollect campaign results On this page 01What advertisers can do 02How to read the internal tools in our examples 03API documentation and downloads Use this guide to Find the right API for the job you want to do. Check what data you can send or receive. See what access each tool requires. Access No account or API key is needed for this guide. No installation is needed to read this guide. What advertisers can do OpenAI advertiser APIs · Guide by Harness · Reviewed 2026-11-08 The arrows show where data goes. This map is based on OpenAI’s documentation. Live account checks are planned. 01 · Advertiser task Set up campaigns and ads Your software → Campaign settings Change the settings the ad system uses to choose and show ads. API to use Create, read, update or delete campaigns, ad groups and ads through api.ads.openai.com/v1 Data available IDs, status, budgets and bids. Context hints (context_hints) describe situations where an ad may be relevant. Creative fields include the title, ad text and destination link (creative.title, creative.body and creative.target_url). What to watch for You can change advertiser settings. Conversation details, ranking scores and individual auction results stay inside the platform. Access Keep the Advertiser API key on your server. The key gives your software access to a specific ad account. Some features require separate access. Campaign setup and management · More API details 02 · Advertiser task Send records of conversions Your server → OpenAI’s measurement system Send a record when someone takes an action you track, such as placing an order. API to use POST https://bzr.openai.com/v1/events?pid=<PIXEL-ID> Data available Send an event ID, the type of action, the time in milliseconds (timestamp_ms), permitted details for matching and other information about the action. The API responds with information about the submission. What to watch for Accepting a record, giving an ad credit for the action and finding out whether the ad caused an extra sale are three separate things. To avoid counting an action twice when you send it from both your website and server, use the same event ID and Pixel ID. Access You need a Pixel ID, which identifies the measurement setup, and a Conversions API key. Get them through Ads Manager or an approved partner setup. Conversions API 03 · Advertiser task Get performance reports OpenAI’s reporting API → Your software Request totals such as impressions, clicks and spend for the account, campaigns or ads you choose. API to use GET /ad_account/insights GET /campaigns/{campaign_id}/insights GET /ad_groups/{ad_group_id}/insights GET /ads/{ad_id}/insights POST /conversions/insights Data available Results grouped by account, campaign, ad group or ad and by time period. Conversion reports have their own definitions and limits. What to watch for General Insights can send a report in batches. A conversion report that is too large needs smaller requests. The reporting example shows how to handle each. Access Keep the Advertiser API key on your server and check your account has the reporting features you need. Add the paths above to https://api.ads.openai.com/v1. Insights reference · More API details How to read the internal tools in our examples OpenAI describes how its system finds, checks and ranks ads before an auction. The exact messages those parts exchange are private. Names like prepare_queries, embed and final_gate belong to our example of how a system like this might work. OpenAI engineering account What the reporting case can answer How often were your ads shown and how much did you spend in the campaigns and dates you chose? Conversation details, relevance scores and the reasons for individual auction results stay inside the platform. API documentation and downloads Use OpenAI’s documentation for the exact requests your software can send. The Harness downloads use made-up examples to explain how you might model ad selection or collect reports. It includes links to OpenAI’s documentation. Harness · reference · v1.0.0Agent reference notes ↓ See where the files came from, how they fit together and how to use them with a coding agent. /learn/system-design/chatgpt-ads-reporti.text: Harness/System design/Reporting example In this guide 01Decide what the report should cover 02Ask Insights for daily campaign results 03Check that you have every batch 04Show what your report is missing 05Can you use this report? 06Interpret credited conversions 07Give an agent a bounded reporting tool 08Reference downloads Back to the track System design · Worked example How to collect ChatGPT Ads reports 11 min readUpdated 9 November 2026Guide preview Build a read-only report of daily spend by campaign. Return the rows you received, their totals, and enough detail to tell whether the report is complete and current. Try the collector locally with fictional data. Live setup is in development and requires verified advertiser API access. On this page 01Decide what the report should cover 02Ask Insights for daily campaign results 03Check that you have every batch 04Show what your report is missing 05Can you use this report? 06Interpret credited conversions 07Give an agent a bounded reporting tool 08Reference downloads Use this guide to Turn a question about daily campaign spend into an Insights request. Collect the result in batches and show which rows, dates, or metrics are missing. Decide whether the result is ready for a decision or safe to pass to an agent. Before you start The examples use HTTP, the rules software follows to send a request over the web and receive a reply. No account or API key is needed for this guide. No installation is needed to read this guide. Explore the case by track System designDefine the report contract Algorithms & dataCheck that you have every batch Software & productionHandle an interrupted report Measurement & MLInterpret credited conversions AI engineeringGive an agent a bounded reporting tool Run the samples locally Decide what the report should cover Start with results by campaign and day for one ad account you have permission to use. Choose the dates and metrics, then keep the account’s time zone, currency and the time you collected the data with the report. A live request needs separate Advertiser API access. Reporting definitions and data updates Harness example of how to collect and save a report 01Request data from your server 02Collect results in batches 03Save data and progress 04Show results and gaps Reports show totals for the campaigns or ads you ask about. Individual conversations, the ads considered for them and their ranking scores stay inside the platform. Keep the Ads API key, a secret your software uses to sign in, on your server. Authentication and account scope Define the result before choosing the interface. Return the requested scope, the scope actually covered, and a status with the reason collection stopped. A subtotal should identify the rows it covers so the caller can tell whether it answers the original question. Explore System design Ask Insights for daily campaign results Insights is the part of the Ads API that returns performance reports. This request asks for one row per campaign per day, with the campaign ID, date, impressions, clicks and spend. Insights request reference Example API request · sample dateshttp GET https://api.ads.openai.com/v1/ad_account/insights aggregation_level=campaign time_granularity=daily fields[]=metadata.readable_time fields[]=campaign.id fields[]=campaign.impressions fields[]=campaign.clicks fields[]=campaign.spend time_ranges[]={"type":"unix_range","start":1793491200,"end":1793577600} # Query values must be URL-encoded. # Authorisation is supplied by your server, never this page. This request covers 1 November 2026 in UTC, the time standard used for the example. The end time is midnight at the start of 2 November, so the request excludes that day. Check the account’s reporting time zone if you want a local calendar day. The download labels OpenAI’s request fields and our own report fields separately. Check that you have every batch Interface How to get the full result General Insights Insights sends results in batches called pages. Save first_id, last_id and has_more. If has_more is true, send the same request with after set to the last_id from that page. Stop when has_more is false. Dedicated conversion report A request to POST /conversions/insights can return error 413 if the report is too large. In that case you get no rows or marker for a next page. Split the request by campaign or other ID, or use shorter date ranges that do not overlap. Local sample collector Track the page markers already seen and the campaign and date pairs already accepted. Stop on a repeated marker or duplicate row and retain the earlier valid batches. Pagination means asking for the next page of the same result. Splitting an oversized conversion report means making several smaller requests and combining their results. Use the rules for the report you asked for. Reporting limits Explore Algorithms & data Show what your report is missing Sample report from Harness · made-up datajson { "reference_kind": "illustrative-reporting-envelope", "account_ref": "sample-account", "status": "partial", "coverage": {"completed_partitions": 2, "expected_partitions": 3}, "missing_partitions": ["campaign-group-c"], "stop_reason": "retry_budget_exhausted" } In this example, two of three batches are ready and the remaining batch is named. Give temporary failures a bounded retry budget. If access is denied or the results cannot be validated, stop and return the batches you already accepted with the reason the report is incomplete. To resume across runs in production, save the original request, accepted batches, and the next cursor. Use the campaign and date to avoid counting a row twice within this report. When figures arrive late, reconcile the newer snapshot for the same scope instead of adding both snapshots together. Try a retry or a partial run The local collector can retry a simulated temporary failure and return accepted rows when it stops early. Each invocation starts a fresh run. Durable checkpoints and live deployment are in development. Explore Software & production Can you use this report? Prepared examples · Fictional data The request in each example Get daily impressions, clicks, spend and credited conversions for campaigns in a fictional UK ad account on 1 and 2 November 2026. Time zone and currency London time, GBP Conversion credit 30 days after a click or one day after a view. Results use the date of the ad interaction. Open an example to see what came back and what you can do with it. Complete reportThe final batch arrived What came back Both batches arrived, giving you three rows. Each row covers one campaign and day. Impressions 2,300 Clicks 64 Spend £36.00 Credited conversions Total unavailable One row shows zero conversions and another has no conversion count. The spend total covers all the returned rows, but there isn’t enough information to add up conversions. What to do next Use the spend total for the requested period. Record when you collected it and check for later updates before using recent figures to make a decision. Empty reportThe request finished with zero rows What came back The first batch was empty and said there were no more batches. There are no totals to show. No rows matched the request. That gives you no spend or conversion figures to interpret. What to do next Check the account, dates and filters. If those are right, report “no rows returned” and keep the totals blank. Partial reportAnother batch is missing What came back The first batch returned two rows and a marker for the next batch. The next batch never arrived. Rows received 2 Spend in rows received £30.50 £30.50 is the subtotal for the rows you have. The spend for the full period is still unknown. What to do next Keep the original dates and filters and use the saved marker to retry the missing batch. If you can’t recover it, label the report partial and carry the gap into any summary. Stale reportAll batches arrived, but the figures are old What came back At a review on 5 November, the team still had a complete report collected on 3 November. They refreshed the same dates and received revised figures. Same reporting dates, two collection times Metric 3 Nov, 09:00 5 Nov, 09:00 Spend £36.00 £36.30 Credited conversions Unavailable 3 Receiving every batch tells you the collection finished. It doesn’t tell you whether the platform has since updated the figures. What to do next Refresh the same request before using the old copy. Use the newer figures for the same dates, and retain both collection times so readers can see what changed. Rejected requestThe requester lacked access What came back In this example, the reporting tool refused the request because the signed-in person didn’t have permission for the selected account. It returned no report. The tool stopped at its access check. There are no figures to interpret for that account. What to do next Check that you selected the right account and ask an account admin to confirm your access. Retry once the account or permission has been corrected. Interpret credited conversions Before comparing reports, check that the account, dates, time zone, currency, and attribution settings match. Check coverage and freshness too. An unavailable conversion count represents missing information. A newer snapshot may have a different count for the same dates. An attributed conversion is an action the platform credits to an ad under its reporting rules. To estimate how many additional sales the campaign caused, define the outcome and compare it with a credible estimate of what would have happened without the campaign. A suitable holdout can provide that comparison. Explore Measurement & ML Give an agent a bounded reporting tool Give the tool one job: read a campaign report within an explicit scope. For a live design, the service should enforce account access and request limits. Return the scope, status, coverage, and freshness alongside the values so an agent can explain an incomplete result before recommending a decision. The local MCP tool reads the bundled fictional reports. Its inputs select a scenario and a page limit. Try the partial scenario and check whether the agent can explain which totals are available and why collection stopped. The collector and adapter run instructions are below. /learn/ai-engineering/verify-small-code-.title: Verify a small code change with an agent · Harness · AI Knowledge Hub
/learn/ai-engineering/verify-small-code-.description: Give an agent a bounded repair, check the changed behaviour, and record the evidence before accepting the change.
/learn/ai-engineering/verify-small-code-.text: Harness/AI engineering/Verify a small code change In this guide 01Give the agent one change and a clear boundary 02Check the broken input and a working input 03Give the reviewer evidence they can use 04Run the versioned Skills example locally Back to the track AI Engineering & Harnesses · Reusable guide Verify a small code change with an agent 5 min readUpdated 10 November 2026 Imagine an internal package installer accepts an empty package identifier. You ask a coding agent to fix it. Before you accept the change, you need evidence that the installer now rejects empty input and still accepts a valid package. On this page 01Give the agent one change and a clear boundary 02Check the broken input and a working input 03Give the reviewer evidence they can use 04Run the versioned Skills example locally Use this guide to Describe the repair and the behaviour it must preserve. Compare what happens before and after the change using a check you trust. Record what passed and what remains unverified. Access No account or API key is needed for this guide. No installation is needed to read this guide. Give the agent one change and a clear boundary Describe the problem in terms you can check. Here, an identifier is the name the installer uses to look up a package. The installer should reject an empty name before it tries to find or install anything. An example request Reject an empty package identifier before lookup. Keep the existing behaviour for valid identifiers. Reproduce the failure, make the smallest change, and show the files changed, the checks you ran, and anything you could not verify. Leave the decision to merge with the reviewer. Check the broken input and a working input Run the checks on the original version to establish what happens today. In this example, empty input reaches the package lookup. Use a fake lookup that records whether it was called, so you can check where validation happens without touching a real package service. Repeat the same checks on the proposed change. Input What the check should show after the change Empty identifier The installer reports an invalid identifier and makes no lookup call. Valid identifier The installer looks up the requested package and returns the expected result. Read the diff, the list of what changed. Check that the agent left the valid path intact. Rerun the checks yourself or use a trusted automated runner. If the agent changed the tests, inspect the new expectations and confirm the empty-input check fails on the original code for the expected reason. A green run is useful only if it still checks the behaviour you care about. Give the reviewer evidence they can use Record the version checked, the command and its observed result, and the limits of the run. For example, a local check with a fake lookup can prove that the installer skips lookup for empty input. It leaves compatibility with a live package service unverified. If a required check could not run, record what blocked it and keep the review open. These checks help you decide whether to accept this one change. To evaluate the agent itself, repeat the exercise across different tasks and failure conditions. The Code Agent’s Playbook in Related reading shows how to design that wider evaluation. Run the versioned Skills example locally The Code Maintenance plugin’s first-use example turns this request into a plan. It runs locally with Node.js 22 and needs only two files from release 0.2.0. Save the download as 0.2.0.tar.gz in a new folder and open a terminal there. Download Code Maintenance Plugin 0.2.0 from Skills Extract the example and run the helperShell tar -xzf 0.2.0.tar.gz scripts/first_use.mjs examples/first-use-input.json node scripts/first_use.mjs examples/first-use-input.json The output includes the proposed check, go test ./internal/installer, and sets merge_authorized to false. The helper prints a plan. To verify a repair, run the proposed check in the installer repository against the candidate change and record what happened. /learn/system-design/when-an-agent-check.title: When an Agent Checkout Times Out · Harness · AI Knowledge Hub
/learn/system-design/when-an-agent-check.description: Follow a stale delivery promise through checkout, then verify whether the merchant created an order before trying again.
/learn/system-design/when-an-agent-check.text: Harness/System design/Agent checkout timeout In this guide 01Recheck the delivery promise 02Trace the checkout timeout 03Look up the order before retrying 04Make a repeat submission safe 05Replay the failures in a test checkout Back to the track System design · Worked example When an Agent Checkout Times Out 7 min readUpdated 18 November 2026Guide preview It’s 12 December. A shopping agent finds an $89 coffee grinder advertised for Christmas delivery. At checkout, the merchant gives a later date. The shopper accepts it, the agent submits the order, and the request times out. The shop might already have the order. What can the agent verify before it takes another action? On this page 01Recheck the delivery promise 02Trace the checkout timeout 03Look up the order before retrying 04Make a repeat submission safe 05Replay the failures in a test checkout Use this guide to Recheck a delivery promise and bind the shopper’s approval to the revised terms. Distinguish a timed-out request from a failed purchase. Use merchant evidence to return an existing order, safely resume the same attempt, or hand off an unresolved case. Before you start The examples use HTTP, the rules software follows to send a request over the web and receive a reply. No account or API key is needed for this guide. No installation is needed to read this guide. Recheck the delivery promise The catalogue still says delivery by 24 December. At checkout, the merchant checks the grinder variant, stock, shipping address and delivery capacity. The current quote is $89 including shipping, with delivery by 28 December. The agent shows the new date and waits. The shopper decides the grinder will still make a good gift and approves the revised terms. Give the quote an identifier and an expiry. In this example, quote q18 records the item, quantity, delivered total and currency, shipping destination and delivery date. The merchant binds the shopper’s approval to those terms. At submission, checkout verifies the approval and reserves the stock and delivery capacity for those terms before it starts payment. If the date or any other material term changes again, show the new quote and ask the shopper to approve it. Where the delivery date comes from The agent can use the catalogue to find a candidate. The merchant’s live checkout supplies the delivery terms for this item and destination. The shopper decides whether those terms still meet their needs. Trace the checkout timeout In this fictional merchant API, approving q18 creates a durable checkout attempt, att-42. The agent saves that reference before submitting. It represents one intended purchase and gives both the checkout service and the agent a way to recognise it after a restart. Scroll across to compare all columns → Time on 12 December What the merchant records What the agent sees 10:02:00 Quote q18 approved. Attempt att-42 is ready. Shopper approved $89 and delivery by 28 December. 10:02:03 Checkout claims att-42 for processing. Submit request sent. 10:02:06 Payment succeeds. Checkout saves order ord-704 against att-42 and commits the order. Still waiting for a reply. 10:02:13 Order ord-704 is confirmed. The request times out. Order outcome unknown to the agent. 10:02:14 Status lookup returns confirmed and ord-704. Agent can show the existing confirmation. At 10:02:13 the agent knows it stopped waiting. The merchant may have received the request, started payment or committed the order. A late email or a pending card authorisation adds evidence but cannot settle all three questions. Ask the merchant for the state of this purchase attempt. Look up the order before retrying The status lookup in the worked exampleHTTP POST /checkout-attempts/att-42/submit → Client times out waiting for the response GET /checkout-attempts/att-42 → 200 OK { "state": "confirmed", "order_id": "ord-704" } This read-only lookup uses the merchant’s checkout record. The server authenticates the caller and checks that they can see this attempt for this shopper and merchant. The reference helps find the record. Access still depends on the caller’s authority. What the lookup establishes What the agent does Confirmed, with an order reference Return the existing order confirmation. End the purchase attempt. Ready, with a current approval Resubmit the same attempt with the same terms if the checkout contract treats repeated submissions as one operation. The delayed first request may still arrive. Processing or unresolved payment Check status again within a short, bounded wait. If it remains unresolved, hand off the attempt reference to merchant support. Quote changed or expired before processing began Verify that the old attempt is terminal with no payment or order. Then get a new quote and shopper approval before starting a replacement. Lookup unavailable or record missing Keep the outcome unknown. Use the merchant’s order history or support to resolve it. What the shopper sees while you check “The checkout timed out. I’m checking whether the shop placed your order.” When the lookup confirms it, report the order reference and the merchant’s delivery terms. If the lookup stays inconclusive, tell the shopper it is still unclear whether the order went through and give them the attempt reference for support. Make a repeat submission safe On the merchant side, claim att-42 atomically before starting payment so that two requests for the same attempt cannot both start it. While one worker is processing, a second request returns that state. After completion, it returns the saved result. Enforce the one-order-per-attempt rule in the order store and reject a repeat submit with changed terms. Keep the same attempt reference across worker restarts. A new reference identifies a separate purchase. Payment has its own failure boundary. A worker can lose the processor’s reply or stop after payment succeeds and before the merchant saves the order. Persist the processor request reference before calling it and use that provider’s idempotency and status rules. Idempotency means repeating the same operation under its contract has the same intended effect as doing it once. If payment is uncertain, keep the attempt open for reconciliation. The merchant matches the processor outcome to its order record and resolves any paid attempt that lacks an order. If the provider’s retry window has expired, verify the existing payment with the provider or hand it off for reconciliation. Stripe’s idempotency rules and retention window This example gives the merchant control of both submit and lookup. In a browser-only checkout, the agent may have only the confirmation screen, the shopper’s order history or merchant support. OpenAI’s Wallet guidance tells the shopper to check for merchant confirmation before trying again when the result is unclear. Use the checks available in that checkout and hand off if they cannot settle the outcome. OpenAI’s Wallet purchase and confirmation guidance Replay the failures in a test checkout Use one grinder, a test payment provider and a way to inspect the merchant’s attempt, payment and order records. Change where the failure occurs and compare the records with what the agent tells the shopper. Failure to introduce Evidence that the checkout handled it Change the promised date after approval and before checkout starts payment. The old approval produces zero orders and zero charges. The agent presents the revised terms. Hold the first submission in transit through the status lookup. Release it alongside the repeat submit. The lookup initially returns ready. Only one request claims att-42. The final records show one order and one successful charge. Drop the response immediately after the merchant commits the order. Lookup returns ord-704. The agent reports it and issues no new submit. The final records show one order and one successful charge. Interrupt the worker after payment succeeds but before the order is saved. The agent reports that it is checking the order. The merchant reconciles the existing payment. The test records show no second charge while the outcome is unresolved. Make status lookup unavailable after a timed-out submit. The agent stops after its read budget and hands off the attempt. It claims neither purchase success nor failure and sends no new submit. The checkout passes when a stale promise cannot authorise a purchase, a lost reply cannot turn one purchase into two, and the shopper hears only what the records support.
